analysis.one_liner: Bans open-market stock buybacks and requires employee-elected directors on a third of corporate boards.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in March 2018, where it never received a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Reward Work Act would prohibit publicly traded companies from buying back their own shares on the open market — the practice by which corporations spend profits repurchasing stock, which lifts the share price and enriches shareholders and executives whose pay is tied to stock. It would also require that one-third of every public company's board of directors be elected by its own employees, one worker one vote, and direct the SEC and NLRB to write rules making those elections fair and phased in within two years. The bill went no further than a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of public companies, who would gain direct representation on corporate boards and a claim on company profits currently recycled into share repurchases. Broader working households also benefit if firms redirect buyback money toward wages, hiring, research, and productive investment instead of financial engineering.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any issuer from purchasing its own equity securities on a national securities exchange, and voids the SEC regulation (Rule 10b-18) that currently gives companies a legal safe harbor to run large open-market repurchase programs.
Requires that no company may register its securities on a national exchange unless at least one-third of its directors are chosen by the company's employees in a one-employee-one-vote election.

Directs the SEC, in consultation with the National Labor Relations Board, to write rules ensuring director elections are fair and democratic and that employee representatives fill a third of boards within two years of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded corporations and their major shareholders, who would lose the ability to spend corporate cash on open-market buybacks that concentrate gains among stockholders, and executives whose compensation depends on stock prices that buybacks lift. Companies would also cede a third of board seats to employee representatives.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers only open-market purchases; the bill expressly leaves tender offers — buybacks made directly to shareholders at a premium — untouched, so determined companies could still return capital through repurchases outside the ban.

Critics of banning buybacks argue that repurchases are a legal way to return excess cash to shareholders, who can reinvest it elsewhere in the economy, and that the market already disciplines firms that buy back stock at inflated prices.

Mandating employee-elected directors for all listed companies is a significant change to corporate governance, and companies could be expected to argue it creates divided loyalties on boards and raises compliance costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gain — giving workers a structural voice in corporate decisions and curbing the practice of recycling profits into stock-price support — is real but diffuse, spread across millions of employees and years. The main costs fall on a concentrated group: large public companies, their biggest shareholders, and executives paid in stock. The bill's biggest design weakness is the tender-offer carve-out, which leaves a clear path for repurchases to continue in another form, so the buyback ban could be partly hollow in practice even though the worker-board mandate would be enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on March 22, 2018, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the Reward Work Act on March 22, 2018, joined by Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Brian Schatz, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Four senators cosponsored the bill — three Democrats and one Independent — all from the same side of the aisle.

The complete action history shows only two actions: introduction and committee referral. The Banking Committee never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large public companies and their shareholders, who kept an unrestricted legal safe harbor for open-market buybacks and kept boards elected entirely by shareholders. Executives whose pay is tied to stock prices also benefited, since buyback-supported share prices were untouched. The Senate Banking Committee's decision to take no action was what preserved the status quo.

sides.party_line_note: All four cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Banking Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill strips them of open-market buybacks — a channel through which they spent record sums in recent years supporting their own share prices — and hands a third of board seats to employee representatives. Their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against workers' interest in a voice and a share of profits.

Buybacks concentrate corporate cash into shareholder payouts; a ban redirects that cash toward wages, investment, and reserves. The current safe-harbor rule (10b-18) that the bill repeals was written to facilitate large repurchases.
Buyback-supported share prices raise the value of executive stock awards; ending open-market repurchases and adding employee directors cuts against that channel of executive pay.
Workers would elect one-third of their company's board under a one-employee-one-vote rule, and capital that would have gone to buybacks could instead support jobs, wages, or investment in the firm.
